column2: I find this research odd because I don’t know what field of study to call this. It’s not computer science. It’s almost like behavioral psychology, but for AI agents instead of humans or animals. That said, I feel like these studies lack a lot of rigor. Or maybe it’s a lack of clear direction. Like, what are we trying to determine here? Because these things often involve advanced AI agents and complex harnesses, but then it sounds like they are given a very minimal prompt. What are we really studying then? Would the outcome be completely different with a different prompt? Can we generalize these results to other models? Different generations of models, different levels of thinking? What if we tried fine-tuning the model to this scenario? Is this fundamentally how any LLM would act, or is this some artifact of our current, generalized fine-tuning?

I started playing the rs-sdk (https://github.com/MaxBittker/rs-sdk) with Claude after seeing it on HN the other day. I haven't looked at the Minecraft experiment but just letting an agent loose in the game and telling it to play did not work well. At first it really did not have a good feel for how the game actually plays and would routinely waste tons of time doing something that makes no sense — very reminiscent of the "four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block" anecdote in this article.

But, after several hours of correcting and directing Claude (build modular, re-usable snippets of useful code rather than one-off scripts for driving, document your learnings for future agents, etc., explicit guidance on playing more optimally) it can now play the game fully on its own. I just gave it a goal to play through the end of the "Legends quest" (nearing end game content, requires playing through lots of complex quests ) and it's breezing through it.

I haven't experimented with swarms of agents yet, but I know if I had tried to create a swarm in 2004scape before the agent was actually good at playing the game, it would have failed horribly. So, I wonder how good the agents they were experimenting with are at Minecraft when playing alone.

I’m not sure there’s too much to take away from this. It seems like a fun experiment, but I find it unsurprising LLMs failed in this context. They used this “mineflayer” wrapper, allowing GPT to read some game state and take actions. Yet the whole time, the game is running and the agents have to sit and process every minute or so. We know that agents cooperate much better in a harness more like bash in a Unix VM attempting some programming task. To conclude from this that agents categorically poorly cooperate and descend into bureaucracy is an overreach. I think anyone working on AI robotics would find this result pretty unsurprising

Humans arrived at a capacity for social cooperation via millions of generations in which it has been a force on reproductive fitness. That created deeply rooted phenotypes like empathy, loyalty, hierarchy, and morality. Even if such concepts can be well described in a statistical model of language, there is no reason to think that they automatically become embedded in motivation. Without that, they may as well be anthropological observations by Martians.

To embed them as motivations, we can embed neural nets within a framework of genetic algorithms, in which successful cooperation is a gate to the next generation. It seems to me that this approach should be not just about creating efficient agent swarms, but should also be at the core of alignment efforts.
